    Kähler geometry

    General complex manifolds

    Edit

    We adopt the following notations in \(\mathbb{C}^n\):

    \begin{equation} z^k=x^k+i y^k, \quad x^k, y^k \in \mathbb{R}. \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} Z=(z^1,...,z^n)=(x^1,...,x^n,y^1,...,y^n). \end{equation}

    The complex structure is given by

    \begin{equation} J_0(Z)=(y^1,...,y^n, -x^1,...,-x^n), \end{equation}

    i.e.,

    \begin{equation} J_0= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_n\\ -I_n & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}

    Set

    \begin{equation} J\left(\partial / \partial x^j\right)=\partial / \partial y^j, \quad J\left(\partial / \partial y^j\right)=-\left(\partial / \partial x^j\right), \quad j=1, \ldots, n . \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} \partial / \partial z^j=\frac{1}{2}\left(\partial / \partial x^j-i\left(\partial / \partial y^j\right)\right), \quad \partial / \partial \bar{z}^j=\frac{1}{2}\left(\partial / \partial x^j+i\left(\partial / \partial y^j\right)\right) . \end{equation}

    Recall that the real representation of \(GL(n;\mathbb{C}) \to GL(2n;\mathbb{R})\) is given by

    \begin{equation} A+iB \to \begin{pmatrix} A & B\\ -B & A \end{pmatrix} . \end{equation}

    A natural one-to-one correspondence(cf. [KN69]):

    \begin{equation} \{ \text{the set of complex structures on} \, \mathbb{R}^{2n} \} \Leftrightarrow GL(2n;\mathbb{R})/GL(n;\mathbb{C}) \end{equation}

    by sending \(S\in GL(2n;\mathbb{R})/GL(n;\mathbb{C})\) into \(SJ_0S^{-1}.\)

    The complex structure on dual space:

    \begin{equation} \la JX,X^* \ra=\la X,JX^* \ra. \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} V^{1,0}=\{X-i J X ; X \in V\} \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} V^{0,1}=\{X+i J X ; X \in V\} \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} V_{1,0}=\left\{X^* \in V^{* c} |\left\langle X, X^*\right\rangle=0,\right. & \left.X \in V^{0,1}\right\}, \\ V_{0,1}=\left\{X^* \in V^{* c} |\left\langle X, X^*\right\rangle=0,\right. & \left.X \in V^{1,0}\right\} . \end{array} \end{equation}

    Hermitian inner product on a real vector space \(V\):

    \begin{equation} h(JX,JY)=h(X,Y), \quad X,Y \in V. \end{equation}

    A natural one-to-one correspondence

    \begin{equation} \{ \text{the set of Hermitian inner products in}\, \mathbb{R}^{2n} \} \Leftrightarrow GL(n;\mathbb{C})/U(n) \end{equation}

    by sending \(S\) to \(h(X,Y)=h_0(SX,SY)\).

    After complex-extending \(h\), we have

    1. \(h(\bar{Z}, \bar{W})=\overline{h(Z, W)} \quad\) for \(Z, W \in V^c\);

    2. \(h(Z, \bar{Z})>0 \quad\) for all non-zero \(Z \in V^c\);

    3. \(h(Z, \bar{W})=0 \quad\) for \(Z \in V^{1,0} \) and \( W \in V^{0,1}\).

    Define a skew-symmetric element

    \[ \boxed{\varphi(X,Y)=h(X,JY),}\]

    then \(\varphi \in \Lambda^{1,1}V^*\) and \(\varphi\) is \(J\)-invariant.

    Let \(\{Z_j\}\) be a basis for \(V^{1,0}\) and \(\{\xi_J\}\) a basis for \(V_{1,0}\). Set

    \begin{equation} h_{j \bar k}=h(Z_j,Z_{\bar k}). \end{equation}

    Then

    1. \(h_{j \bar k}=\bar{h}_{k \bar j}\)

    2. \(\varphi=-i\sum_{j,k=1}^n h_{j \bar k}\xi^j \wedge \bar{\xi}^k\)

    i.e.,

    \begin{equation} \varphi(Z, W)=-i \sum_{j, k=1}^n h_{j \bar k}\left(\xi^j(Z) \bar{\xi}^k(W)-\xi^j(W) \bar{\xi}^k(Z)\right) . \end{equation}

    The torsion of \(J\):

    \begin{equation} N(X,Y)=2\{ [JX, JY] - [X, Y] - J[X, JY] - J[JX, Y] \}, \quad X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}(M). \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} N_{j k}^i=2 \sum_{h=1}^{2 n}\left(J_i^h \partial_h J_k^i-J_k^h \partial_h J_j^i-J_h^i \partial_j J_k^h+J_h^i \partial_k J_j^h\right). \end{equation}

    The complex differential forms on an almost complex manifold \(M\) of dimension \(2n\):

    \begin{equation} d \mathfrak{C}^{p, q} \subset \mathfrak{C}^{p+2, q-1}+\mathfrak{C}^{p+1, q}+\mathfrak{C}^{p, q+1}+\mathfrak{C}^{p-1, q+2} . \end{equation}

    An infinitesimal automorphism is a vf. \(X\) s.t. \(L_XJ=0,\) equivalently,

    \begin{equation} [X,JY]=J[X,Y], \quad \forall Y \in \mathfrak{X}(M) \end{equation}

    On any complex manifold \(M\):

    1. The Lie algebra of infinitesimal automorphisms of the complex structure \(J\) is isomorphic with the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields, the isomorphism being given by

      \[X \to Z=\frac{1}{2}(X-iJX) .\]

      Note that we can write

      \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2}(X-i J X)=\sum_{j=1}^n f^j\left(\partial / \partial z^j\right), \quad \frac{1}{2}(Y-i J Y)=\sum_{j=1}^n g^j\left(\partial / \partial z^j\right) , \end{equation}

      but \(f^j, g^i\) are not necessarily holomorphic functions.

    2. \(M\) admits an almost complex affine connection (\(\nabla J=0\)) such that its torsion \(T\) is given by

      \[N=8T. \]

    3. \(T(J X, J Y) -J(T(J X, Y))-J(T(X, J Y))-T(X, Y)=-\frac{1}{2} N(X, Y)\)

    4. \(R(X,Y)\circ J=J\circ R(X,Y)\)

    On any almost Hermitian manifold \((M,J,g)\):

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} 4 g\left(\left(\nabla_X J\right) Y, Z\right)= 2 d \Phi(X, J Y, J Z)-2 d \Phi(X, Y, Z) +g(N(Y, Z), J X) , \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    where the fundamental 2-form \(\Phi(X,Y)=g(X,JY)\).

    Some simple calculation

    Edit

    Set

    \[ Z_j=\frac{1}{2}(X_j-iY_j), \quad \bar Z_j=\frac{1}{2}(X_j+iY_j),\]

    then

    \[ X_j=Z_j+\bar Z_j, \quad Y_j=i(Z_j-\bar Z_j). \]

    For any bilinear operator

    \[ A(X_j,X_j)+A(Y_j,Y_j) = 2\{A(Z_j,\bar Z_j) +A(\bar Z_j, Z_j) \},\]

    \[ A(Z_j,\bar Z_j)=\frac{1}{4}\{ A(X_j,X_j)+A(Y_j,Y_j) \}-\frac{i}{4}\{ A(X_j,Y_j)+A(Y_j,X_j) \} ,\]

    \[ X_jX_j+Y_jY_j=2(Z_j \bar Z_j+\bar Z_j Z_j)\]

    \[ Z_j \bar Z_j=\frac{1}{4}(X_jX_j+Y_jY_j)+ \frac{i}{4}(X_jY_j-Y_jX_j).\]

    Hermitian metric on Kähler manifolds

    Edit
    Remark
    Edit
    1. Hermitian fiber metric in this case is a map

    \[h: \Gamma\left(T_J M\right) \times \Gamma\left(T_J M\right) \rightarrow C^{\infty}(M ; \mathbb{C})\]

    that satisfies all of the following:

    • \(h\) is bilinear over \(C^{\infty}(M ; \mathbb{R})\);
    • \(h(J X, Y)=i h(X, Y)\);
    • \(h(X, J Y)=-i h(X, Y)\);
    • \(h(Y, X)=\overline{h(X, Y)}\);
    • \(h(X, X)>0\) at points where \(X \neq 0\).
    1. Write \(h=g+i\omega\), where \(g=Re(h), \omega =Im(h)\), then
    • \(g\) is a Riemannian metric. (since \(g(X, Y)=\frac{1}{2}(h(X, Y)+\overline{h(X, Y)})=\frac{1}{2}(h(X, Y)+h(Y, X))\).)
    • \(\omega (X,Y)=g(X,JY), g(X,Y)=\omega (JX,Y)\) and \(g, \omega \) are both \(J\)-invariant.
    1. Define a Hermitian metric \(\la, \ra\) by

    \begin{equation} \boxed{\la Z,W\ra=g(Z,\bar W).} \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    In local holomorphic coordinates,

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} g & =g_{j \bar{k}} d z^j \otimes d \bar{z}^k+g_{\bar{j} k} d \bar{z}^j \otimes d z^k \\ & =2 g_{j \bar{k}}\left(\frac{d z^j \otimes d \bar{z}^k+d \bar{z}^k \otimes d z^j}{2}\right) \\ & =2 g_{j \bar{k}} d z^j d \bar{z}^k. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    If \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector fields, written locally as \(X=X^j \partial_j+X^{\bar{j}} \partial_{\bar{j}}\) and \(Y=Y^j \partial_j+Y^{\bar{j}} \partial_j\), then

    \[ g(X, Y)=g_{j \bar{k}}\left(X^j Y^{\bar{k}}+Y^j X^{\bar{k}}\right), \]

    and \(g(X, X)=2 g_{j \bar{k}} X^j X^{\bar{k}}\).

    Proposition
    Edit

    Given the isomorphim \(\xi: T_JM \to T'M\) by \(\xi(X)=X-iJX\), then

    \[ \la \xi(X), \xi(Y)\ra=2h(X,Y) .\]

    We could have avoided this discrepancy by adding a factor of \(\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\) to the definition of \(\xi \).

    Proposition
    Edit

    In holomorphic coordinates, for sections \(Z, W\) of \(T^{\prime} M\), we have

    \[ \langle Z, W\rangle=g\left(Z^j \partial_j, W^{\bar{k}} \partial_{\bar{k}}\right)=g_{j \bar{k}} Z^j W^{\bar{k}}, \]

    On the other hand, if \(X\) and \(Y\) are real, decomposed as \(X=Z+\bar{Z}\) and \(Y=W+\bar{W}\) with \(Z, W \in \Gamma\left(T^{\prime} M\right)\), then

    \[ \langle X, Y\rangle=g_{j \bar{k}}\left(Z^j W^{\bar{k}}+W^j Z^{\bar{k}}\right) \]

    In particular, for \(X=Z+\bar{Z}\), this yields

    \[ |X|^2=|Z+\bar{Z}|^2=|Z|^2+|\bar{Z}|^2=2|Z|^2=2 g_{j \bar{k}} Z^j Z^{\bar{k}} . \]

    Proposition (Raising and lowering, the musical isomorphim)
    Edit

    Define for a complex \(X\), \(X^b(Y)=g(X, Y), \forall Y \in T_{\mathbb{C}}M\). Then for \(Z \in T'M\), we have

    \[Z_{\bar k} = g_{j \bar k}Z^{j}, \quad g^{j \bar k}Z_{\bar k} = Z^{j}.\]

    Kähler metrics(kn)

    Edit

    The metric \(g\) is Kählerian if \(\Phi\) is closed. For a Kähler manifold, we have

    \[ R(JX, JY) = R(X, Y), \quad \operatorname{Ric}(JX, JY) = \operatorname{Ric}(X, Y) = \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr} \{ J \circ R(X, JY) \}. \]

    Set

    \[ Z_{\alpha} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z^{\alpha}}, \quad Z_{\bar{\alpha}} = \bar{Z}_{\alpha} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}^{\alpha}}; \]

    \[ g_{AB} = g(Z_A, Z_B), \quad A, B = 1, \dots, n, \bar{1}, \dots, \bar{n}. \]

    Thus \(g_{\alpha \beta} = g_{\bar{\alpha} \bar{\beta}} = 0\), and

    \[ \boxed{g = ds^2 = 2 \sum_{\alpha, \beta}^n g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} dz^{\alpha} d\bar{z}^{\beta}.} \]

    Note that here \(dz^{\alpha} d\bar{z}^{\beta}\) is the symmetric product, that's why factor 2. Also

    \[ \boxed{\Phi = -i \sum_{\alpha, \beta = 1}^n g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} dz^{\alpha} \wedge d\bar{z}^{\beta}.} \]

    For \(g\) to be Kählerian:

    \[ \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}}}{\partial z^{\gamma}} = \frac{\partial g_{\gamma \bar{\beta}}}{\partial z^{\alpha }}, \quad \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}}}{\partial \bar{z}^{\gamma}} = \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \bar{\gamma}}}{\partial \bar{z}^{\beta}}. \]

    For an affine connection, set

    \[ \nabla_{Z_B} Z_C = \sum \Gamma_{BC}^A Z_A. \]

    Then

    \[ \bar \Gamma_{BC}^A = \Gamma_{\bar{B} \bar{C}}^{\bar{A}} \quad \text{with convention $\bar{\bar \alpha} = \alpha$.}. \]

    For \(\nabla\) to be almost complex:

    \[ \Gamma_{B \gamma}^{\bar\alpha} = \Gamma_{B \bar{\gamma}}^{\alpha} = 0. \]

    For an almost complex \(\nabla\) to be torsion free:

    \[ \Gamma_{\beta \gamma}^{\alpha} = \Gamma_{\gamma \beta}^{\alpha}, \quad \Gamma_{\bar{\beta} \bar\gamma}^{\bar{\alpha}} = \Gamma_{\bar\gamma \bar{\beta}}^{\bar{\alpha}}, \]

    and other \(\Gamma_{BC}^A = 0\).

    In particular, for a Kähler manifold:

    \[ \sum_{\alpha} g_{\alpha \bar{\epsilon}} \Gamma_{\beta \gamma}^{\alpha} = \frac{\partial g_{\bar\epsilon \beta}}{\partial z^{\gamma}}, \quad \sum_{\alpha} g_{\bar\alpha \epsilon} \Gamma_{\bar{\beta} \bar \gamma}^{\bar{\alpha}} = \frac{\partial g_{\epsilon \bar{\beta}}}{\partial \bar{z}^{\gamma}}. \]

    Set (as before)

    \[ R(Z_C, Z_D) Z_B = \sum_A K_{BCD}^A Z_A, \]

    \[ K_{ABCD} = g \left( R(Z_C, Z_D) Z_B, Z_A \right), \]

    then

    \[ K_{ABCD} = \sum_E g_{AE} K^E_{BCD}. \]

    From

    \[ \Rightarrow K^{\alpha}_{\bar{\beta} CD} = K^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\beta CD} = 0, \]

    thus

    \[ K^{\alpha}_{\bar{\beta} CD} = K^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\beta CD} = 0, \]

    and by symmetry of tensor \(R\):

    \[ K_{\alpha \beta CD} = K_{\bar \alpha \bar{\beta} CD} = 0, \]

    \[ K^{A}_{B \gamma \delta} = K^{A}_{B \bar{\gamma} \bar \delta} = 0, \quad K_{AB \gamma \delta} = K_{AB \bar{\gamma} \bar \delta} = 0. \]

    Consequently, the only non-zero components are

    \[ K^{\alpha}_{\beta \bar \gamma \delta}, \quad K^{\alpha}_{\beta \gamma \bar{\delta}}, \quad K^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\bar \beta \bar \gamma \delta}, \quad K^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\bar \beta \gamma \bar{\delta}}, \]

    \[ K_{\alpha \bar{\beta} \gamma \bar \delta}, \quad K_{\bar \alpha \beta \bar{\gamma} \delta}, \quad K_{\alpha \bar{\beta} \bar{\gamma} \delta}, \quad K_{\bar{\alpha} \beta \gamma \bar{\delta}}. \]

    We obtain

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:80} K^{\alpha}_{\beta \gamma \bar \delta} = -\partial \Gamma^{\alpha}_{\beta \gamma} / \partial \bar z^{\delta}, \end{equation}

    \[ K_{\alpha \bar{\beta} \gamma \bar{\delta}} = \frac{\partial^2 g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}}}{\partial z^{\gamma} \partial \bar{z}^{\delta}} - \sum_{\tau, \epsilon} g^{\bar{\epsilon} \tau} \frac{\partial g_{\alpha \bar{\epsilon}}}{\partial z^{\gamma}} \frac{\partial g_{\bar \beta \tau}}{\partial \bar{z}^{\delta}}, \]

    where \((g^{\alpha \bar{\beta}})\) inverts \((g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}})\) such that \(\sum_{\beta} g^{\alpha \bar{\beta}} g_{\gamma \bar{\beta}} = \delta^{\alpha}_{\gamma}\).

    Ricci curvature:

    \[ K_{AB} = \sum_C K^C_{ACB} \]

    Denote \(G = \det(g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}})\), then

    \[ \frac{\partial G}{\partial z^{\alpha}} = G \sum_{\beta, \gamma} g^{\beta \bar{\gamma}} \frac{\partial g_{\beta \bar{\gamma}}}{\partial z^{\alpha}}. \]

    Thus

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:92} \sum_{\gamma} \Gamma^{\gamma}_{\alpha \gamma} = \frac{\partial \log(G)}{\partial z^{\alpha}}, \end{equation}

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:93} K_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} = -\frac{\partial^2 \log(G)}{\partial z^{\alpha} \partial \bar{z}^{\beta}}. \end{equation}

    Also

    \begin{equation} Rc = 2 R_{j \bar{k}} dz^j d\bar{z}^k, \quad S = 2 g^{j \bar{k}} R_{j \bar{k}}. \end{equation}

    Remark
    Edit

    Note that \(\eqref{eq:92}\) holds for real Riemannian manifolds if we set \(G = (\det(g_{ij}))^{\frac{1}{2}}\), but \(\eqref{eq:93}\) is far from the truth.

    Ricci form (defined by \(\rho(X, Y) = \operatorname{Ric}(X, JY)\)):

    \[ \rho = -i \sum K_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} dz^{\alpha} \wedge d\bar{z}^{\beta} = i \partial \bar{\partial} \log(G), \]

    by \(\eqref{eq:93}\). And this means that

    \[ d\rho = 0. \]

    Let \(F\) be a real-valued function in a coordinate neighborhood of a complex manifold \(M\) and set

    \[ g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} = \frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial z^{\alpha} \partial \bar{z}^{\beta}}, \]

    which is Hermitian since \(F\) is real. If it's positive definite, then \(2 \sum_{\alpha, \beta = 1}^n g_{\alpha \bar{\beta}} dz^{\alpha} d\bar{z}^{\beta}\) is a Kähler metric by (75). Conversely, a Kähler metric can be written in this form locally. We have

    \[ K_{\alpha \bar{\beta} \gamma \bar{\delta}} = \frac{\partial^4 F}{\partial z^{\alpha} \partial \bar{z}^{\beta} \partial z^{\gamma} \partial \bar{z}^{\delta}} - \sum_{\epsilon, \tau} g^{\bar{\epsilon} \tau} \frac{\partial^3 F}{\partial \bar{z}^{\epsilon} \partial z^{\alpha} \partial z^{\gamma}} \frac{\partial^3 F}{\partial z^{\tau} \partial \bar{z}^{\beta} \partial \bar{z}^{\delta}}. \]

    Example (\(\mathbb{C}^n,K=0\))
    Edit

    Kähler form and metric:

    \[ \omega = -\frac{i}{2} \sum_j dz^j \wedge d\bar{z}^j = -\sum_j dx^j \wedge dy^j, \quad g = \sum_j dz^j d\bar{z}^j, \]

    since \(g \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j} \right) = \delta_{kj}\), and thus, \(g \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}^j} \right) = \frac{1}{2} \delta_{kj}\).

    Example (\(\mathbb{CP}^n, K=1\) )
    Edit

    Define the affine coordinates \((U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\). \(U_{\alpha} = \{ [w]=[w^0,...,w^n] \in \mathbb{CP}^n : w^{\alpha} \neq 0 \}\); \(\varphi_{\alpha} : U_{\alpha} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n\)

    \[ \varphi_{\alpha}([w^0, \dots, w^n]) = \left( \frac{w^0}{w^{\alpha}}, \dots, \frac{w^{\alpha-1}}{w^{\alpha}}, \frac{w^{\alpha+1}}{w^{\alpha}}, \dots, \frac{w^n}{w^{\alpha}} \right), \]

    then

    \[ \varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(z^1, \dots, z^n) = [z^1, \dots, z^{\alpha-1}, 1, z^{\alpha}, \dots, z^n], \]

    \[ \varphi_{\alpha} \circ \varphi_{\beta}^{-1}(z^1, \dots, z^n) = \left( \frac{z^1}{z^{\alpha}}, \dots, \frac{\hat{z}^{\alpha}}{z^{\alpha}}, \dots, \frac{1}{z^{\alpha}}, \dots, \frac{z^n}{z^{\alpha}} \right), \quad \alpha <\beta. \]

    Set

    \[ \quad \Theta_H |_{U_{\alpha}} = \bar{\partial} \partial \log \frac{|w^{\alpha}|^2}{|w|^2}. \]

    In affine coordinates \((z^1, \dots, z^n) \leftrightarrow [z^1, \dots, 1, \dots, z^n]\) on \(U_{\alpha}\),

    \[ \Theta_H \big|_{U_{\alpha}} = \bar{\partial} \partial \log \frac{1}{1 + |z|^2} = \partial \bar{\partial} \log(1 + |z|^2), \]

    which implies

    \[ \Theta_H = \frac{\sum_j dz^j \wedge d\bar{z}^j}{1 + |z|^2} - \frac{\sum_{j,k} \bar{z}^j z^k \, dz^j \wedge d\bar{z}^k}{(1 + |z|^2)^2}. \]

    Let \(\omega_{FS}\) be the following closed real \((1,1)\)-form:

    \[ \quad \omega_{FS} = -2i \Theta_H, \]

    then

    \[ g_{j \bar{k}} = 2 \left( \frac{\delta_{jk}}{1 + |z|^2} - \frac{\bar{z}^j z^k}{(1 + |z|^2)^2} \right). \]

    Or

    \[ ds^2 = 4 \frac{\left( 1 + \sum z^{\alpha} \bar{z}^{\alpha} \right) \left( \sum dz^{\alpha} d\bar{z}^{\alpha} \right) - \left( \sum \bar{z}^{\alpha} dz^{\alpha} \right) \left( \sum z^{\alpha} d\bar{z}^{\alpha} \right)}{\left( 1 + \sum z^{\alpha} \bar{z}^{\alpha} \right)^2}. \]

    Example (\(\mathbb{B}^{2n}\),\(K=-1\) )
    Edit

    Define

    \[ \omega_{\text{CH}} = 2i \partial \bar{\partial} \log(1 - |z|^2), \]

    then

    \[ g_{j \bar k}= 2 \left( \frac{\delta_{jk}}{1 - |z|^2} + \frac{\bar{z}^j z^k}{(1 - |z|^2)^2} \right).\]

    Or

    \[ ds^2 = 4 \cdot \frac{\left( 1 - |z|^2 \right) \sum_j dz^j d\bar{z}^j + \left( \sum_j \bar{z}^j dz^j \right) \left( \sum_k z^k d\bar{z}^k \right)}{\left( 1 - |z|^2 \right)^2}. \]

    Proposition (Volume for Kähler metric)
    Edit

    \[ dV_g = \frac{(-1)^n}{n!} \omega^n = \frac{(-1)^n}{n!} \omega \wedge \cdots \wedge \omega. \]

    Proof
    Edit

    Note that

    \[ (\omega_{(k)})^k = k! \, dx^1 \wedge dy^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^k \wedge dy^k, \]

    where

    \[ \omega_{(k)}=\sum_{j=1}^{k} dx^j \wedge dy^j .\]

    Theorem (Normal coordinate for Kähler metric)
    Edit

    For every \(a \in M\), there exists a holomorphic coordinate chart centered at \(a\) such that

    \[ \boxed{g_{j \bar{k}}(a) = \frac{1}{2} \delta_{jk} \quad \text{and} \quad d(g_{j \bar{k}}) \big|_a = 0.} \]

    Theorem (Characterizations of Kähler Metrics)
    Edit

    Let \(M\) be a complex manifold and \(g\) be a Hermitian metric on \(M\). We use the following notations:

    • \(\omega\) is the fundamental 2-form of \(g\).

    • \(h = g + i \omega\).

    • \(\nabla\) is the Levi-Civita connection of \(g\).

    • \(\nabla^{(h)}\) is the Chern connection of \(h\) on \(T_J M\).

    • \(\xi : T_J M \to T'_J M\) is the isomorphism \(\xi(v) = v - i J v\).

    The following statements are equivalent:

    1. \(g\) is Kähler (i.e., \(d\omega = 0\)).

    2. For every \(p \in M\), there exists a real-valued function \(u\) on a neighborhood \(V\) of \(p\) such that \(\omega |_V = i \partial \bar{\partial} u\).

    3. In every holomorphic coordinate chart, \(\partial_j g_{ k \bar{l}} = \partial_k g_{j \bar{l}}\) for all \(j, k, l\).

    4. For every \(a \in M\), there exists a holomorphic coordinate chart centered at \(a\) such that

      \[ g_{j \bar{k}}(a) = \frac{1}{2} \delta_{jk} \quad \text{and} \quad d(g_{j \bar{k}}) \big|_a = 0. \]

    5. In every holomorphic coordinate chart, all Christoffel symbols of \(g\) are identically zero except those of types \(\Gamma^l_{jk}\) and \(\Gamma^{\bar{l}}_{\bar j \bar{k}}\).

    6. \(\nabla\) restricts to the Chern connection on \(T_J M\) with respect to the Hermitian fiber metric \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\).

    7. For every real or complex vector field \(X\), \(\nabla_X\) maps \(\Gamma(T' M)\) to itself.

    8. \(\nabla J \equiv 0\).

    9. \(\nabla \omega \equiv 0\).

    10. \(\nabla \xi \equiv 0\).

    11. \(\nabla\) is compatible with the holomorphic structure on \(T_J M\).(That's \(\nabla^{(0,1)}=\bar \partial_E\), where \(E=T_JM\). )

    12. \(\nabla^{(h)} = \nabla\).

    13. \(\nabla^{(h)}\) is torsion-free.

    Curvatures(lee)

    Edit
    Remark
    Edit

    Note that the John M Lee's notations are different from ours, for example, he defined

    \begin{equation} R(\partial _i, \partial _j)\partial_k=R_{ijk}^l \partial_l \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} R(x,y,z,w)=g(R(x,y)z,w) \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R_{ijk}^m, \end{equation}

    and the Bianchi identity is

    \begin{equation} R_{ijkl}+R_{jkil}+R_{kijl}= 0, \end{equation}

    and the sectional curvature is

    \begin{equation} K(x,y)=\frac{R(x,y,y,x)}{|x|^2|y|^2-g(x,y)^2}. \end{equation}

    Compare to Sec.

    In this section, we refer most content from his book, but adapting to our notations as in previous!

    A useful identity on any Kähler manifold:

    \begin{equation} \boxed{ R(Z,\bar Z, W,\bar W)=-4\{R(X, Y,X,Y)+R(X,JY,X,JY) \}=-4R(X,JX,Y,JY),} \end{equation}

    where

    \[Z=X-iJX, \quad W=Y-iJY \in T'M.\]

    Also, if let \(X=Re(Z), Y=Im(Z)\), then

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} R(X,Y,X,Y)=\frac{1}{4}R(Z,\bar Z,\bar Z,Z)\\ |X|^2|Y|^2-g(X,Y)^2=\frac{1}{4}|Z|^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    Definition (holomorphic sectional curvature)
    Edit

    \[ H(Z):= \frac{R(Z,\bar Z, \bar Z, Z)}{|Z|^4}.\]

    Definition (holomorphic bisectional curvature)
    Edit

    \begin{equation} H(p,p') := R(X, JX, Y, JY) =R(X, Y, X, Y) + R(X, JY, X, JY), \end{equation}

    where \(p,p'\) are two \(J\)-invariant planes and \(X,Y\) are unit in \(p,p'\) respectively. Or equivalently,

    \begin{equation} H(p,p')=B(Z, W)=\frac{R (Z, \bar{Z}, \bar{W},W)}{|Z|^2|W|^2}. \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    \(H(Z)=K(Re(Z),Im(Z)) =K(X,JX)\), thus the definition coincides with KobayashiNomizu's (Also true for holomorphic bisectional curvature).

    Proposition
    Edit

    \(B(Z,W)=K(Re(Z),Re(W))+K(Re(Z),Im(W))\) .

    Proposition
    Edit

    A Kähler metric \(g\) has constant holomorphic sectional curvature \(c\) iff

    \begin{equation} R_{j \bar{k} l \bar{m}}=-\frac{1}{2} c\left(g_{j \bar{k}} g_{l \bar{m}}+g_{l \bar{k}} g_{j \bar{m}}\right) , (\text{under complex vector basis}) \end{equation}

    iff

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} R(X, Y, Z, W)=\frac{c}{4}[ & g(X, Z) g(Y, W)-g(X, W) g(Y, Z) \\ & +g(X, J Z) g(Y, J W)-g(X, J W) g(Y, J Z) \\ & +2 g(X, J Y) g(Z, J W)] \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    for all real vectors \(X,Y,Z,W\). If this's the case, we have

    \begin{equation} R(X, J X, Y, J Y)=\frac{c}{2}\left[g(X, X) g(Y, Y)+g(X, Y)^2+g(X, J Y)^2\right] , \end{equation}

    and

    \begin{equation} R(X, J X, X, J X)=c|X|^2. \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    If \(H(Z)=c\), i.e., \(g\) has constant holomorphic sectional curvature \(c\), then the range of (holomorphic bisectional curvature) \(H(p,p')\) is \([\frac{c}{2},c]\). Here the value \(c/2\) is attained when \(p\) is perpendicular to \(p'\) whereas the value \(c\) is attained when \(p=p'\).

    Proposition
    Edit

    Let \(M\) be a complex manifold of dimension \(n\), and let \(g\) be a Kähler metric on \(M\) with constant holomorphic sectional curvature \(c\).\ (a) Let \(v, w \in T_x M\) be a pair of orthonormal vectors. One can show that the (ordinary) sectional curvature of \(g\) in the direction of the plane spanned by \((v, w)\) is given by

    \[ K (v, w)=\frac{1}{4} c\left(1+3\langle v, J w\rangle^2\right) . \]

    (b) Also, one can show that if \(n \geq 2\), then at each point of \(M\), the (ordinary) sectional curvatures of \(g\) take on all values between \(\frac{1}{4} c\) and \(c\), inclusive. Conclude that \(M\) cannot have constant sectional curvature unless it is flat.

    Proposition (Symmetric properties for Kähler metrics)
    Edit

    \[ R(X,Y)\circ J = J \circ R(X,Y)\]

    \[ Ric(JX,JY)=Ric(X,Y)=\frac{1}{2} \trace(J \circ R(X,JY)) \]

    \[ R(J X, J Y, Z, W)=R(X, Y, J Z, J W)=R(X, Y, Z, W) \]

    For \(X,Y,Z,W \in T'M\):

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} R(W, X, \cdot, \cdot) & =R(\cdot, \cdot, W, X)=0, \\ R(\bar{W}, \bar{X}, \cdot, \cdot) & =R(\cdot, \cdot, \bar{W}, \bar{X})=0 \\ R (W, \bar{X}, Y, \bar{Z}) & =R(Y, \bar{X}, W, \bar{Z}), \\ R (W, \bar{X}, Y, \bar{Z}) & =R(W, \bar{Z}, Y, \bar{X}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    \section{Curvature forms (chenweihuan)}
    Set \((1 \leq \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \dots \leq n)\)

    \[ \nabla \frac{\partial}{\partial z_{\alpha}} = \omega^{\beta}_{\alpha} \frac{\partial}{\partial z_{\beta}}, \quad \nabla \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\alpha}} = \theta^{\beta}_{\alpha} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\beta}} + \theta^{n + \beta}_{\alpha} \frac{\partial}{\partial y_{\beta}}, \]

    \[ \nabla \frac{\partial}{\partial y_{\alpha}} = \theta^{\beta}_{n + \alpha} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\beta}} + \theta^{n + \beta}_{n + \alpha} \frac{\partial}{\partial y_{\beta}}. \]

    Then

    \[ \theta^{\beta}_{\alpha} = \theta^{n + \beta}_{n + \alpha}, \quad \theta^{\beta}_{n + \alpha} = -\theta^{n + \beta}_{\alpha}, \quad \omega^{\beta}_{\alpha} = \theta^{\beta}_{\alpha} + i \theta^{n + \beta}_{\alpha}, \]

    which is, in fact, the condition for \(\nabla \) to be almost complex.

    Now ( with different range of indices!) set

    \[ \Omega^j_i = d\omega^j_i - \omega^k_i \wedge \omega^j_k, \quad \Theta^{\beta}_{\alpha} = d\theta^{\beta}_{\alpha} - \theta^{\gamma}_{\alpha} \wedge \theta^{\beta}_{\gamma}; \quad 1 \leq j, i, k \leq n, \quad 1 \leq \alpha, \beta, \gamma \leq 2n. \]

    Then

    \[ \boxed{\Omega^j_i = \Theta^j_i + \sqrt{-1} \, \Theta^{\bar{j}}_i,} \]

    \[ \Theta^{\bar{j}}_{\bar i} = \Theta^j_i, \quad \Theta^j_{\bar{i}} = -\Theta^{\bar{j}}_i, \quad \bar{i} := n + i, \quad \bar{j} := n + j. \]

    Also

    \[ R^{\bar{j}}_{\bar i \gamma \delta} = R^j_{i \gamma \delta}, \quad R^j_{i \gamma \delta} = -R^{\bar{j}}_{i \gamma \delta}, \]

    \[ R^{\beta}_{\alpha \bar i \bar{j}} = R^{\beta}_{\alpha i j}, \quad R^{\beta}_{\alpha \bar{i} j} = -R^{\beta}_{\alpha i \bar j}, \]

    where \(R\) is applied to \(\left\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\alpha}}, 1 \leq \alpha \leq 2n \right\}\).

    Remark
    Edit

    Note that if we choose a unitary frame, then we have, in addition, that

    \begin{equation} \omega^\beta _\alpha =-\bar \omega ^\alpha _\beta ,\quad \Omega^\beta _\alpha =-\bar \Omega ^\alpha _\beta . \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    Set

    \[ K^j_{ikl} = \left( R^j_{ikl} + R^{\bar{j}}_{i\bar kl} \right) + \sqrt{-1} \left( R^j_{ik\bar l} + R^{\bar{j}}_{i \bar k\bar l} \right), \]

    then

    \[ \boxed{\Omega^j_i = \frac{1}{2} K^j_{ikl} \, dz^k \wedge d\bar{z}^l,} \]

    \[ R \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}^l} \right) \frac{\partial}{\partial z^i} = \frac{1}{2} K^j_{ikl} \frac{\partial}{\partial z^j}. \]

    That is \(\left( \frac{1}{2} K^j_{ikl} \right)\) is the matrix of complex linear transformation \(R \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}^l} \right): T_{(1,0)} M \to T_{(1,0)} M\) under the basis \(\left\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial z^i} \right\}\).

    Remark
    Edit

    One can also prove

    \[ K^j_{ikl} = K^j_{kil}. \]

    In fact, one can further prove

    \[ K^j_{ikl} = -2 \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}^l} \left( h^{j\bar p} \frac{\partial h_{i\bar p}}{\partial z^k} \right), \]

    where \(h_{i\bar p} = g \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial z^i}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar z^p} \right) = \frac{1}{2} \left( g \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^p} \right) + \sqrt{-1} g \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^p} \right) \right)\). (The notation \(K^j_{ikl}\) here is exactly \(2 K^j_{ik \bar l}\) in \(\eqref{eq:80}\) !)

    Bundle-valued forms

    Edit

    Let \(E\to M\) be a smooth complex vector bundle.

    Several natural wedge product operations:

    1. \(\alpha \in \mathscr{E}^q (M), \beta \otimes \sigma \in \mathscr{E}^{q'} (M;E)\)

      \[ \alpha \wedge (\beta \otimes \sigma) = (\alpha \wedge \beta) \otimes \sigma \]

    2. \(\alpha \otimes \varphi \in \mathscr{E}^q (M;E^*), \beta \otimes \sigma \in \mathscr{E}^{q'} (M;E)\)

      \[ (\alpha \otimes \varphi) \wedge (\beta \otimes \sigma) =\varphi (\sigma ) (\alpha \wedge \beta) \in \mathscr{E}^{q+q'}(M) \]

    3. \(\alpha \otimes A \in \mathscr{E}^q (M;End(E)), \beta \otimes B \in \mathscr{E}^{q'} (M;Edn(E))\)

      \[ (\alpha \otimes A) \wedge (\beta \otimes B) =(\alpha \wedge \beta) \otimes (A\circ B) \in \mathscr{E}^{q+q'}(M;End(E)) \]

    4. \(\alpha \otimes A \in \mathscr{E}^q (M;End(E)), \beta \otimes \sigma \in \mathscr{E}^{q'} (M;E)\)

      \[ (\alpha \otimes A) \wedge (\beta \otimes \sigma ) =(\alpha \wedge \beta) \otimes A(\sigma ) \in \mathscr{E}^{q+q'}(M;E) \]

    Example
    Edit

    In a local basis, \(\{s_j\}\) is a frame of \(E\), and \(\{\epsilon \}\) is its dual frame. Then

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \omega \wedge \eta & =\left(\omega_k^j \otimes s_j \otimes \varepsilon^k\right) \wedge\left(\eta_m^l \otimes s_l \otimes \varepsilon^m\right) \\ & =\left(\omega_k^j \wedge \eta_m^l\right) \otimes\left(\delta_l^k s_j \otimes \varepsilon^m\right) \\ & =\left(\omega_k^j \wedge \eta_m^k\right) \otimes\left(s_j \otimes \varepsilon^m\right) \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    That's matric product: in an expression like \(\omega_k^j\) we always interpret the upper index as the row number and the lower index as the column number. Likewise, if \( \gamma =\gamma^m \otimes s_m \),

    \begin{equation} \omega \wedge \gamma =(\omega^j_k \wedge \gamma^k) \otimes s_j. \end{equation}

    Definition (Cauchy–Riemann Operator)
    Edit

    If \(E\) is holomorphic, then the following is well-defined:

    \begin{equation} \bar \partial_E \sigma |_{U}= (\bar \partial \sigma^j )\otimes s_j, \quad \forall \sigma \in \mathscr{E}^{p,q}(M,E). \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    Suppose \(M\) is a complex manifold and \(E \to M\) is a holomorphic vector bundle. There are operators \(\bar{\partial}_E : \mathscr{E}^{p,q}(M; E) \to \mathscr{E}^{p,q+1}(M; E)\) satisfying the following properties:

    • For \(\sigma \in \mathscr{E}^{0,0}(M; E) = \Gamma(E)\), \(\bar{\partial}_E \sigma = 0\) if and only if \(\sigma\) is a holomorphic section.

    • For \(\alpha \in \mathscr{E}^{p,q}(M)\) and \(\beta \in \mathscr{E}^{p',q'}(M; E)\),

      \[ \bar{\partial}_E (\alpha \wedge \beta) = \bar{\partial} \alpha \wedge \beta + (-1)^{p+q} \alpha \wedge \bar{\partial}_E \beta. \]

    • For \(\gamma \in \mathscr{E}^{p,q}(M; E^*)\) and \(\beta \in \mathscr{E}^{p',q'}(M; E)\),

      \[ \bar{\partial} (\gamma \wedge \beta) = \bar{\partial}_E \gamma \wedge \beta + (-1)^{p+q} \gamma \wedge \bar{\partial}_E \beta. \]

    • \(\bar{\partial}_E \circ \bar{\partial}_E = 0\).

    • If \(\alpha \in \mathscr{E}^{p,q}(M; E)\) satisfies \(\bar{\partial}_E \alpha = 0\), then in a neighborhood of each point there exists \(\beta \in \mathscr{E}^{p,q-1}(M; E)\) such that \(\bar{\partial}_E \beta = \alpha\).

    1. [KN69] Shoshichi Kobayashi and Katsumi Nomizu. Foundations of differential geometry. Vol. II. Volume No. 15 of Interscience Tracts in Pure and Applied Mathematics. Interscience Publishers John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York-London-Sydney, 1969.
